clinicalPearls: A group of disorders in which target tissues resist aldosterone despite high aldosterone and renin, causing salt wasting rather than salt retention

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 has a renal autosomal dominant form (NR3C2 mineralocorticoid receptor) that is milder and often improves with age, and a systemic autosomal recessive form (epithelial sodium channel subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) that is severe and lifelong
Typically presents in the neonate with failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis
The systemic recessive form also affects sweat glands, colon and airways and can mimic cystic fibrosis with salty sweat and respiratory symptoms
Biochemistry shows hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, high plasma renin and markedly elevated aldosterone, in contrast to adrenal insufficiency where aldosterone is low
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (Gordon syndrome, WNK/KLHL3/CUL3) is the mirror image, with hyperkalaemia, hypertension and low renin
Management centres on sodium supplementation and control of hyperkalaemia, since mineralocorticoids are ineffective because the defect is downstream of the hormone
reference.pathophysiology: Mineralocorticoid resistance encompasses the pseudohypoaldosteronism syndromes, in which the distal nephron fails to respond to aldosterone despite elevated hormone levels. In the autosomal dominant renal form of type 1, heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in NR3C2 (the mineralocorticoid receptor) blunt renal sodium reabsorption. In the autosomal recessive systemic form, mutations in the epithelial sodium channel subunits abolish sodium transport across multiple aldosterone-responsive epithelia including kidney, colon, sweat and salivary glands, and lung. Impaired sodium reabsorption drives salt wasting, volume depletion and secondary activation of renin and aldosterone, while reduced electrogenic sodium uptake impairs potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Type 2 (Gordon syndrome) instead reflects overactive distal sodium chloride reabsorption from mutations in the WNK-kinase pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Primary adrenal insufficiency or salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, where aldosterone is low
Cystic fibrosis, for the systemic form with salty sweat and respiratory features
Secondary or transient pseudohypoaldosteronism from urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy in infants
Gordon syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2) for the hyperkalaemic hypertensive phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine and venous blood gas showing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, both high in type 1
Urinary sodium and potassium to demonstrate renal salt wasting
Sweat chloride testing to help distinguish the systemic form from cystic fibrosis, noting both can raise sweat chloride
Renal tract imaging to exclude secondary or transient pseudohypoaldosteronism
Genetic testing of NR3C2, the epithelial sodium channel subunit genes, and the WNK pathway genes for type 2
redFlags: Neonatal salt-wasting crisis with severe hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrhythmia
Failure to thrive and dehydration unresponsive to mineralocorticoid replacement
Respiratory compromise in the systemic form mimicking cystic fibrosis
reference.prognosis: The autosomal dominant renal form of type 1 is generally mild and tends to improve with age as dietary sodium intake rises, whereas the recessive systemic form requires lifelong aggressive salt supplementation and carries greater morbidity; with careful electrolyte management most patients grow and develop normally.
pitfalls: Confusing it with adrenal insufficiency and giving mineralocorticoid, which is ineffective because resistance lies downstream
Missing transient or secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism due to infant urinary tract infection or obstruction
Mislabelling the systemic form as cystic fibrosis on the basis of a raised sweat chloride
Failing to distinguish salt-wasting type 1 from hypertensive type 2 (Gordon syndrome)
management: Replace sodium generously with oral sodium chloride supplementation, the mainstay for salt-wasting pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1
Control hyperkalaemia with dietary potassium restriction and potassium-binding cation-exchange resins
Correct the metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate or citrate
Treat acute salt-wasting crises with intravenous saline and emergency measures for severe hyperkalaemia
In the systemic recessive form, provide skin care and airway and respiratory management for the cystic-fibrosis-like manifestations
Manage pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (Gordon syndrome) differently, with dietary sodium restriction and a thiazide diuretic
Monitor growth, electrolytes and acid-base status regularly, expecting the dominant renal form to ease with age
Offer genetic testing and counselling to define the subtype and guide family screening
